article.headline: Semiconductor Stocks, Adjusted for Inflation, Look a Lot Like 2000
article.lede: A monthly, inflation-adjusted chart of semiconductor stocks has reached a level of divergence from its long-run trend that closely mirrors the spring of 2000 — the last time the sector looked this extended. Then, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index collapsed 82 percent over the following 31 months. The question now is whether the underlying demand story — artificial intelligence infrastructure rather than telecom fiber — is meaningfully different.
article.body:
The image is a monthly, logarithmic chart of the *Philadelphia Semiconductor Index* (SOX) — a thirty-component benchmark of chip designers, manufacturers, and distributors — divided by the U.S. Consumer Price Index. By expressing semiconductor stocks in constant purchasing-power terms, the ratio lets three decades of boom-and-bust cycles be compared on equal footing. A four-year *exponential moving average* (EMA) runs beneath it as a long-cycle trend filter: roughly the span of one complete semiconductor industry cycle, from inventory glut to peak demand and back. What @Axis_Balance is pointing to is the gap between the current ratio and that average — a departure that, on a log scale, now looks nearly indistinguishable from the spring of 2000.

The underlying numbers justify the concern. The SOX hit an all-time high of 10,624 on May 1, 2026, after rallying 41 percent in four weeks — the strongest four-week advance since the March 2000 dot-com peak. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, which tracks the index, logged its best monthly return in its 25-year history in April 2026, at +40.4 percent. The SOX's *relative strength index* (RSI) reached 85, a reading associated with extreme overbought conditions, while the index traded 48 percent above its 200-day moving average. Counterintuitively, **NVIDIA** (NVDA) — the dominant supplier of AI training accelerators — underperformed its own sector during April's surge, gaining roughly 22 percent against the broader benchmark's 41.

The valuation echo is harder to dismiss than the chart pattern alone. At the dot-com peak, the SOX sector traded at 8.8 times book value; today it trades at roughly 10 times — a higher starting multiple. The semiconductor sector comprised approximately 7 percent of total U.S. market capitalization in 2000; it now accounts for roughly 14 percent. In the last cycle, the SOX ran more than sevenfold from its 1998 lows to a nominal peak of 1,362, then collapsed 82 percent to 209 over 31 months. The four-year EMA on the SOX/CPI ratio, covering one full industry cycle in real terms, shows today's deviation above trend as broadly comparable in magnitude to that departure.

The structural question is whether this time the demand driver is permanent. In 2000, the underlying shock was telecom infrastructure: carriers spent more than $500 billion building fiber-optic networks, creating what looked like secular demand for semiconductors and proved to be a one-time build-out. The present-day analog is AI infrastructure capex — the five largest cloud providers planned a combined 36 percent year-on-year increase in infrastructure spending for 2026, with analysts at IDC projecting global semiconductor revenues approaching $1 trillion for the year. Wedbush analyst Dan Ives has argued there are “no cracks in AI demand on the chips/hardware or software front.” The counter-case — which this chart implicitly makes — is that whether the demand driver is fiber or GPUs matters less than the pattern: late-cycle acceleration, multiples priced for permanence, and a ratio that has diverged from its long-run real trend by as much as it did the last time this chart looked like this.

concepts.definition: A chart pattern in which an asset's price accelerates nearly vertically — typically on surging volume and with minimal pullbacks — before reversing sharply downward. Technicians identify it by parabolic price action, momentum indicators diverging from new price highs, and a reversal that erases much of the preceding gain rapidly. It is associated with the final, euphoric stage of a bull-market cycle.

A capitalization-weighted index of 30 companies involved in the design, distribution, manufacturing, and sale of semiconductors, maintained by Nasdaq OMX. It is the primary benchmark for the sector's stock-market performance and serves as a proxy for the health of the global chip industry across economic cycles.

A type of moving average that weights recent data more heavily than older observations, making it more responsive to recent price changes than a simple average. On a monthly chart, a four-year (48-month) EMA spans roughly one complete semiconductor industry cycle and acts as a long-run trend benchmark; significant deviation above it signals an unusual departure from cycle norms.

A momentum oscillator measuring the speed and magnitude of recent price changes on a 0-to-100 scale. Readings above 70 are conventionally overbought; above 80–85, they signal extreme conditions that have historically preceded short-term pullbacks in cyclical sectors. The SOX reached RSI 85 in late April 2026.

A valuation multiple comparing a company's (or sector's) stock-market value to its accounting book value — the net assets on the balance sheet. A ratio of 10 times book means investors are paying $10 for every $1 of net assets, implying a large premium for expected future earnings. Historically, extreme price-to-book levels in cyclical industries have correlated with subsequent long-term underperformance.

A chart scale where each equal vertical distance represents the same percentage change rather than the same absolute change. This makes it possible to compare proportional moves across different time periods and magnitudes — a doubling from 100 to 200 occupies the same vertical space as a doubling from 1,000 to 2,000. It is standard practice for comparing long-run boom-and-bust cycles in rapidly growing sectors.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.
